questions.q: What is ZudoJS?
questions.explain: ZudoJS takes over the backend jobs from What a framework does: lifecycle, dependency injection, routing, configuration, validation, errors, data access, security, testing and project structure.
options: A database for storing JSON documents on Node.js
A backend framework for TypeScript on Node.js, made of small packages
A front-end library for building pages in the browser
A new programming language that compiles to JavaScript

questions.q: How is ZudoJS published?
questions.explain: Each package owns one job. You install only the ones you use, and most of them also work on their own in a project that is not a ZudoJS app. The zudojs package on npm is only the CLI; it gives you the commands zudojs and zudo.
options: As one big npm package called zudojs that contains the whole framework
As two packages: a server and a client
As 38 small packages named @zudojs/…, plus the command-line tool zudojs (short command zudo)
As a program you download from the website, not from npm

questions.q: Your app needs validation and errors, but no queue and no tenancy. What do you install?
questions.explain: ZudoJS is split so you install only what you need. queue arrives when you have background jobs, tenancy when you serve several customers from one app.
options: All 38 @zudojs packages, because they only work together
Only the packages you use, such as @zudojs/schema and @zudojs/errors
Only the zudojs CLI, which contains every package inside it
Nothing: ZudoJS is already built into Node.js

questions.q: ZudoJS packages sit on "shelves". What is the rule?
questions.explain: Dependencies point down only. The bottom packages depend on no other ZudoJS package, and the top ones build on everything below.
options: A package may use packages on higher shelves, never lower ones
A package may use packages on lower shelves, never higher ones
A package may only use packages on its own shelf
A package may use any other package, on any shelf

questions.q: What does the shelf rule give you?
questions.explain: If dependencies only point down, no package can end up needing itself through others. That keeps each package independent, like the domain layer in Clean architecture.
options: Every package is guaranteed to be under 100 lines
Packages can be installed in any order with npm
No cycles, so each package can be built, tested and understood on its own
Every package can run in the browser as well as in Node.js

questions.q: Which package sits at the bottom, used by almost every other package?
questions.explain: Because almost every package uses @zudojs/errors, an error from any package is a BaseError with a status code and a stable code. @zudojs/types sits beside it.

questions.q: After sign-up, you want to send a welcome e-mail in the background. Which package is for that?
questions.explain: A queue runs background jobs, so the sign-up request can answer at once while the e-mail is sent later, with retries.

questions.q: Only admins may delete books. Which package decides who may do what?
questions.explain: @zudojs/auth finds out who is asking. @zudojs/permissions decides whether that user may do the action. You need both checks, but "only admins" is a permission rule.

questions.q: You must read DATABASE_URL and stop the app if it is missing. Which package?
questions.explain: Reading and checking settings is the job of @zudojs/config. The database package uses the setting, but config reads it and fails early when it is missing.

questions.q: You want to count requests per second on a dashboard. Which package?
questions.explain: Observability is about seeing inside a running app: metrics like requests per second, and traces. The logger writes what happened, line by line.

questions.q: On a request's path, which packages find out who is asking, and whether they may do it?
questions.explain: auth finds the user, like requireUserId did in the BookStore, and permissions decides what that user may do. schema checks the body, and errors turns failures into status codes.

questions.q: What does "one description, two uses" mean for NewBookSchema?
questions.explain: In the BookStore you wrote an interface and a parser separately, and they could disagree. A schema is one description that gives both the runtime check and the type.
options: It checks the data both in the browser and on the server
It checks data at runtime, and Infer turns it into the TypeScript type
It can parse both JSON text and JavaScript objects
It creates both the database table and the HTTP route

questions.q: The example registers BookService with scope: ContainerScope.SINGLETON. What does that mean?
questions.explain: Singleton means one shared instance. That is why container.resolve(BOOKS) === books printed true: all code sees the same list of books.
options: A new BookService is created every time someone resolves the token
The service can only be resolved once, then it throws
It is created the first time it is asked for, and everyone gets that same instance
The service is created before the container exists

questions.q: Why can one instanceof BaseError check read the status code of both a SchemaError and your own NotFoundError?
questions.explain: Every ZudoJS package builds its errors on @zudojs/errors, so they share one family. One check handles errors from any package the same way.
options: Because instanceof works on any object that has a statusCode
Because both errors are created by @zudojs/schema
Because JavaScript converts every error into a BaseError

questions.q: Which command starts the development server and restarts it when you save a file?
questions.explain: zudojs dev is for working on your code. zudojs build compiles the project to JavaScript for production, and create makes a new project.

questions.q: You want a new OrderService file in the right folder of your project. Which command?
questions.explain: generate adds a service, controller, repository, module and more. add adds a whole feature, such as database or queue, to an existing project.

questions.q: Something is wrong with your setup, and you want the CLI to check your Node.js, packages and project. Which command?
questions.explain: doctor checks for problems. info only shows the CLI version and the project's ZudoJS packages.

questions.q: You are starting a new project with a small team. Which architecture should you choose?
questions.explain: A monolith is the default and what this course uses. Microservices add a lot of operational work, and pay off only when parts must scale or deploy on their own.
options: A monolith: one application, one codebase, one process
Microservices, so every part can scale on its own from day one
A modular monolith with a gateway in front of it
Microservices, because they need less operational work

questions.q: What is a modular monolith?
questions.explain: It is still one program to deploy, but modules like catalog, orders and users keep clear boundaries. You get order in the code without running many services.
options: Several separate applications, each with its own database
One deployable application, split into strict modules that talk through clear interfaces
A monolith where every module may reach into every other module's code
A monolith that runs one process per module

questions.q: When do microservices make sense?
questions.explain: Microservices are separate applications talking over the network, usually behind a gateway. The healthy path is monolith, then modular monolith, then microservices only where needed.
options: When you are starting out and want to move fast
When the whole team is one or two people
When different parts must scale or be deployed independently, by different teams
Whenever the app has more than one database table

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: .trim() removes the spaces around the title before the other checks run, and the result is the cleaned value. The price stays in cents.

questions.q: The client sends an extra field. What does this print?
questions.explain: An object schema keeps only the keys it describes. The unknown isAdmin is dropped, so it can never slip into your data.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Bad input is the client's fault, so the SchemaError carries status 400. It extends BaseError, so the instanceof check matches it.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A NotFoundError knows its own status code (404) and a stable machine-readable code. You only give it the message.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The schema's error and your NotFoundError both extend BaseError. A plain Error does not; it is not part of the ZudoJS error family.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: With SINGLETON, the container creates one BookService and returns that same instance on every resolve.

questions.q: How many times does the factory run? What does this print?
questions.explain: Registering only says how to build the service. The container builds it the first time someone asks for the token, and as a singleton it reuses it after that.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Asking for a token nobody registered is a mistake in the app's wiring, not in the client's request, so it is a 500. It is still a BaseError, like every ZudoJS error.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: safeParse never throws: it returns success: false and a list of issues. .int() refuses 12.5, and the issue's path names the field, priceCents.

questions.q: A title of only spaces. What does this print?
questions.explain: .trim() runs first, so " " becomes "" and fails .min(1). " a " becomes "a", which passes.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: find returns undefined for id 9, so the service throws a NotFoundError. It carries 404 and the message you gave it.

questions.q: Two users try to register the same e-mail. What does this print?
questions.explain: 409 Conflict means the request clashes with the current state, such as a duplicate e-mail. Like every ZudoJS error, it is a BaseError with a stable code.

questions.q: A form sends the price as text. What does this print?
questions.explain: schema.number() accepts only real numbers. The string "1200" is refused, not quietly converted, so type mistakes are caught at the edge.

questions.q: This time the scope is TRANSIENT. What does this print?
questions.explain: A transient registration builds a new instance on every resolve. SINGLETON is what you want for a shared service like BookService.

questions.q: Finish NewTaskSchema with @zudojs/schema: title is a string, trimmed, 1 to 100 characters; priority is a whole number from 1 to 5.
questions.explain: Chain the checks: schema.string().trim().min(1).max(100) and schema.number().int().min(1).max(5). Put trim() before min(1) so a title of only spaces is refused.

questions.q: Finish findByTitle: return the book with exactly that title, or throw a NotFoundError from @zudojs/errors with the message No book called "TITLE".
questions.explain: Use find, and throw when it returns undefined. The NotFoundError brings the 404 with it, so no code has to remember the number.

questions.q: Register CounterService under the COUNTER token as a singleton, using useFactory. Then every resolve shares one counter.
questions.explain: container.register(COUNTER, { useFactory: () => new CounterService() }, { scope: ContainerScope.SINGLETON }). Every resolve returns the same instance, so the count goes 1, 2, 3.

questions.q: Finish toResponse(error). For a BaseError, return { status: error.statusCode, code: error.code }. For anything else, return { status: 500, code: "internal_error" }.
questions.explain: One instanceof BaseError check covers errors from every ZudoJS package. An unknown error gets a generic answer, so its message (here about a password) never reaches the client.

questions.q: Finish add(input) in BookService: parse input with NewBookSchema, give the book the next id (1, 2, …), store it and return it.
questions.explain: Parse first: if the input is bad, parse throws before anything is stored. The schema drops the client's id: 77, so the service always chooses the id.

questions.q: Finish checkShelves(shelf, deps). shelf gives each package's shelf number (0 is the bottom). deps lists what each package uses. Return a message "A may not use B" for every dependency that is not on a lower shelf.
questions.explain: A package may only use packages on a strictly lower shelf. config and schema share shelf 1, so that use is refused too; errors using http points up, which would create cycles.
questions.expected:
[ 'config may not use schema' ]
[ 'errors may not use http', 'config may not use schema' ]

questions.q: Finish createBook(body) without try/catch: use NewBookSchema.safeParse. On success return { status: 201, book: data }. On failure return { status: 400, fields: [...] } with the path of each issue joined by ".".
questions.explain: safeParse returns { success, data } or { success: false, issues } instead of throwing. Each issue's path names the field, so the client learns what to fix.
